segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who are under the yoke as slaves must regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be blasphemed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who have believing masters must not look down on them because they are brothers; instead they must serve them all the more, because those who benefit from their good service are believers and beloved. Teach these things and urge them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone teaches something different and does not agree with the sound words, those of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the teaching that accords with godliness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that person is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing, but is sick with a craving for controversies and battles over words. From these come envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and constant friction among people who are corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And godliness with contentment is indeed a great means of gain;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for we brought nothing into the world, and neither can we carry anything out of it;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but having food and clothing, we will be content with these.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare and many senseless and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the love of money is a root of all evils. Some, reaching for it, have been led astray from the faith and have pierced themselves with many pains.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and for which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who testified to the good confession before Pontius Pilate,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to keep the commandment unstained and beyond reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which the blessed and only Sovereign will display at the right time—the King of kings and Lord of lords,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no human being has seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal power. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Charge those who are rich in the present age not to be arrogant or to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: charge them to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, turning away from the profane empty talk and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: by professing it, some have missed the mark concerning the faith. Grace be with you.

notes.phrase: those who benefit from their good service
notes.note: The Greek can be read two ways. On the reading adopted here, which most modern translations share, the masters are the ones who receive the benefit of the slaves’ service. The verb can also mean “devote oneself to”, which would give “those who devote themselves to doing good are believers and beloved”. The word for “good service” normally described the benefaction of a superior, so applying it to a slave’s work is striking.

notes.traditional: doting about; has an unhealthy craving
notes.note: The verb means to be ill, and it is set against the “sound” (literally “healthy”) words of verse 3. The letter pictures correct teaching as health and the opponents’ obsession with disputes as a disease. Scholars differ on how strongly the medical image was felt, but the pairing here suggests it is deliberate.

The Greek word was a prized term in popular philosophy, especially among Stoics and Cynics, for self-sufficiency: needing nothing beyond what one has. The related verb appears in verse 8 (“we will be content”). The sentence also plays on verse 5: the opponents think godliness is a “means of gain”, and the writer agrees, in a sense they did not intend.

notes.phrase: and neither can we carry anything out of it
notes.traditional: and it is certain we can carry nothing out
notes.note: The connecting word in the earliest manuscripts normally means “because” or “that”, which gives an awkward logic (“we brought nothing in because we can take nothing out”). Later manuscripts smooth this by adding “it is clear that” or “it is true that”, which lies behind the King James rendering. Most modern translations, as here, treat the connection as a loose “and” or “so”.

notes.traditional: the root of all evil; a root of all kinds of evil
notes.note: The Greek has no article with “root”, and it can be read as “a root” or, in a proverbial saying like this, “the root”. The following phrase is literally “of all the evils”; many modern versions soften it to “all kinds of evil”, but the Greek does not say “kinds”. The saying resembles proverbs about greed current in the period and is best heard as a sweeping maxim, not a precise claim about the cause of every wrong.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Here, in a list of qualities to pursue, the word means upright conduct, doing what is right. “Righteousness” is the standard rendering; some translators prefer “justice”.

The verb and its noun come from the world of athletic contests, where competitors struggled for a prize, and were widely used for any strenuous effort. The picture is of a contest in the arena as much as of warfare; “compete in the good contest” would also be a fair rendering.

The adjective is formed from the word for “age”. In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of its kind as well as its unending length. Verse 19 calls the same thing “the life that is truly life”, and verse 17 contrasts it with “the present age”.

The preposition can mean “in the presence of”, pointing to Jesus’ testimony at his trial, or “in the time of”, as in the creeds’ “under Pontius Pilate”, which would point to his whole witness culminating in his death. Most translations take it as “before”, and that reading is followed here.

The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, not the word for “world” used in verse 7. New Testament writers share the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come, and that contrast is the point here: wealth belongs to this age, while verse 19 looks to “the future”. Several modern versions also render “present age”.

notes.traditional: science falsely so called; what is falsely called knowledge
notes.note: The opponents evidently claimed a special “knowledge” (Greek gnosis), and the word for “contradictions” may refer to their debating propositions or counter-arguments. Whether this is connected with the Gnostic movements known from the second century is disputed; the letter gives too little detail to be sure. The King James “science” meant “knowledge” in older English.

In the earliest manuscripts “you” is plural, which suggests the letter, though addressed to Timothy, was expected to be heard by the congregation. Many later manuscripts have the singular “you” and add “Amen”, readings reflected in the King James Version.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the Pastorals, Acts and 2 Peter; translators vary among godliness, piety, devotion and religion, and the ordinary Greek sense (proper reverence toward the divine) is not obvious from “godliness”.
Occurs across the whole New Testament and versions vary among slave, servant and bondservant, which changes how readers picture both the institution and the metaphor.
Frequent in the Pastorals and rendered either “teaching” or “doctrine”; the choice should be uniform so that readers see the same word in “sound teaching” passages.

A near-technical term in the Pastorals and 2 Thessalonians for Christ’s manifestation, variously rendered appearing, manifestation or epiphany, and it had strong associations with divine and imperial appearances.
The noun and its verb recur in Paul, the Pastorals and Hebrews, and versions vary among fight, struggle, contest and race, which obscures the shared athletic image.
